dedupe_keys.name: harris county texas unequal access to grocery stores during hurricane harvey from location based data

description: This case study measures how access to grocery stores changed for different neighbourhoods of Harris County, Texas, before, during and after Hurricane Harvey in 2017. The authors, researchers at Texas A&M University, used high-resolution location-based data from mobile devices, spatial network analysis and dynamic clustering, and published the work in an open-access journal article. Three access indicators were computed for each area and phase of the disaster: the number of unique stores visited, the average trip time and the average distance to stores, standing for redundancy, rapidity and proximity of access. Coverage is one county at fine spatial resolution across the preparation, impact and short-term recovery periods. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution licence; the device data are commercial and not published. Caveats: location data under-represent some groups, visits are a proxy for access, and the results describe one hurricane. The study found that food desert status and store counts alone miss much of the disparity, that flooding hit socially vulnerable populations hardest, and that high-income areas had better access during preparation because residents visited more stores and travelled farther. Simulation uses: observed recovery of food access for validating food supply disruption and equity models after floods. Related records: the Harris County food pantry access study (case_study-harris-county-food-pantry-access-after-flooding) and the Hurricane Harvey food access survey (data-designsafe-harvey-food-access-impact-survey) cover the same event.
